title: Modi Lands in New Zealand. He Brings a Trade Deal, 5,000 Visas, and a 'Butter Chicken Tsunami.'
excerpt: The first Indian PM visit in forty years arrives with a free-trade agreement that opens markets and creates visa pathways — but also ignites a fierce domestic backlash over immigration.
body:
For the first time in forty years, an Indian Prime Minister has landed in New Zealand.

Narendra Modi arrived in Auckland on Friday for a two-day state visit that comes loaded with more diplomatic freight than the trade deal it is supposed to celebrate. The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement, signed in April and still awaiting parliamentary passage, promises to reshape how two distant economies trade — and how many Indians can work in a country where their growing presence has become a lightning rod.

The last Indian PM to visit was Rajiv Gandhi, in 1986. The world those two countries occupied is almost unrecognisable now. India is the world's fifth-largest economy. New Zealand's Indian-born population has surged into one of the country's fastest-growing communities, with deep roots in healthcare, IT, agriculture, and small business.

But that growth has collided with a volatile domestic debate. And the FTA sits right at the centre of it.

## What the Deal Actually Does

The numbers are straightforward. From the day the agreement takes effect, 100 per cent of Indian exports will receive duty-free access to New Zealand. Going the other way, 57 per cent of New Zealand's exports to India — wood products, processed timber, wool, sheep meat — will enter tariff-free on day one, with the rest phased in over time until 95 per cent of New Zealand goods face zero or reduced tariffs.

For India, the wins are in textiles, leather, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, and automobiles. For New Zealand, the prize is access to one of the world's fastest-growing consumer markets. India has also, for the first time under any FTA, agreed to open its market to New Zealand apples and honey. Tariffs on manuka honey will be reduced.

New Zealand's Prime Minister Christopher Luxon framed it in the simplest possible terms on Thursday: "57% of everything we export to India will be tariff free from day one."

India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal called it "India's best-ever market access and services offer."

Two-way goods and services trade currently sits at roughly $2.4 billion. Both sides expect the FTA to push that figure significantly higher.

## The 5,000 Visas — And the 'Butter Chicken Tsunami'

But the FTA is not just about tariffs. Embedded in the agreement is a dedicated visa pathway for up to 5,000 Indian professionals over three years through Temporary Employment Entry visas, targeted at occupations where New Zealand has genuine skill shortages — doctors, nurses, teachers, ICT professionals, engineers, and even culturally specific roles like Ayurvedic medicine practitioners, yoga instructors, and Indian chefs. A separate working holiday scheme allows up to 1,000 young Indians aged 18 to 30 to visit annually.

These provisions have been the most politically incendiary element of the deal.

Shane Jones, a minister from the coalition partner New Zealand First, described the immigration components as a "butter chicken tsunami" — a comment that drew immediate and widespread condemnation. Party leader Winston Peters went further, calling the entire deal "madness" and a "disgraceful sellout." New Zealand First triggered the coalition's formal agree-to-disagree mechanism, allowing it to vote against the FTA while remaining in government.

The Labour opposition ultimately provided the votes to ensure passage, with leader Chris Hipkins saying: "This is not the deal Labour would have negotiated, but we value our relationship with India and the positive contributions of our Indian communities."

The political backdrop extends beyond parliament. In recent months, anti-Indian sentiment in New Zealand has surfaced in online forums, community complaints, and sporadic protests. Just days ago, as Modi addressed a packed arena in Melbourne during the Australia leg of his trip, a small group of far-right protesters outside shouted anti-immigration slogans and held banners calling for the expulsion of Indians — though they were heavily outnumbered by flag-waving Indian supporters.

## What NRIs Are Watching

For the roughly 240,000 people of Indian origin in New Zealand and the far larger Indian communities across Australia, the UK, and North America, the visit carries significance beyond any single trade clause.

The FTA includes safeguards: the temporary visas have no pathway to permanent residence or citizenship, carry a three-year cap, and require a three-year stand-down before reapplication. India's chief trade negotiator Vangelis Vitalis told parliament the provisions were "very carefully drafted" and that India "well understood" the limits.

But the symbolism matters. An Indian Prime Minister on New Zealand soil for the first time in four decades, backed by a trade deal that explicitly creates visa pathways for Indian professionals — this is the kind of bilateral infrastructure that the diaspora has long wanted. Whether it survives the political currents is another question.

New Zealand's Indian community has organised a major reception in Auckland, with organisers preparing for attendance that could exceed 13,000 people. The event, planned under the banner "Kia Ora Modi," is expected to be one of the largest Indian diaspora gatherings ever held in the country.

## The Bigger Picture

Modi's New Zealand stop is the final leg of a three-nation Indo-Pacific tour that began in Indonesia — where he signed a BrahMos missile deal — and continued through Australia, where he secured a landmark uranium export agreement and addressed thousands at a Melbourne arena.

The pattern is consistent: India is deepening its strategic footprint across the Indo-Pacific through defence, energy, trade, and diaspora engagement, all at once. New Zealand, with its growing Indian population and newly signed FTA, is the latest piece in that architecture.

Whether the "butter chicken tsunami" rhetoric fades into an embarrassing footnote or hardens into something uglier will depend less on what Modi says in Auckland and more on what happens in New Zealand's parliament, its labour market, and its streets in the months ahead.

*Sources: Reuters, Hindu Business Line, The Bridge Chronicle, The NZ Today, Asia Media Centre, IANS, Farmers Weekly NZ*
